5531.t: From βρέχω (brékhō, “to rain”) + -η (-ē, abstract noun suffix).

5514.t: Probably onomatopoeic; see also βάσκειν (báskein) and βάσκανος (báskanos), which are potentially related.

5561.t: Thematicization of δάμνημι (dámnēmi, “to subdue”). Cognates include Sanskrit दाम्यति (dāmyati), Latin domō.

5572.t: From an earlier unattested *δημιο-ϝεργός (*dēmio-wergós), from a univerbation of δήμια ἔργα (dḗmia érgă).

5555.t: Uncertain. Commonly linked to γρυπός (grūpós, “hook-nosed; aquiline”), which is from Proto-Indo-European *ger- (“to turn, twist, bend, wind”), related to Old English crumb, crump (“bent, crooked”), Old High German krump.

5505.t: Uncertain. Beekes mentions that derivation from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eysd- (“to laud, honour”) + *-ōs, though semantically attractive, is formally difficult, as the expected form would be **αἰζώς (**aizṓs).

5538.t: From Proto-Hellenic *génewyom, from the root of γένυς (génŭs, “jaw, mouth”).

5534.t: According to Beekes, probably of onomatopoeic origin. A connection with Armenian կորկ (kork, “dirt”) remains very doubtful.

5535.t: Unknown, but Beekes suggests a Pre-Greek origin in view of the suffix -υχος. Often connected with βότρυς (bótrus, “bunch of grapes”).

5565.t: From Proto-Indo-European *dwey-mós, from *dwey- (“fear”). Compare δέος (déos), Latin dirus, Old Armenian երկն (erkn).

5536.t: Probably from Egyptian bꜣkt (“oil flask”). Beekes dismisses any relation with Latin fiscus (“basket”) and βαυκάλιον (baukálion, “jug, pitcher”).

5517.t: Unknown. According to Beekes the word is perhaps Pre-Greek, in view of the variation -λλ-/-λ-.

5537.t: Unknown; a candidate for Pre-Greek origin.

5541.t: From the root of γίγνομαι (gĭ́gnomai, “to be born”) from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁-.

5525.t: A reduplicated formation from the zero grade of Proto-Indo-European *gʷeh₂- (“to step, go”) with -άζω (-ázō), functioning as a factitive (causative) present meaning “to make or cause to go”.

5558.t: Inherited from Proto-Indo-European *gómos, a derivation of *gem- (“to press together; to grasp”) and so related to γέμω (gémō, “to be full of”), γέντο (génto, “he/she grasped”), Latin gemō (“to sigh, groan”) and Proto-Slavic *žęti (“to press, squeeze”).

5570.t: From δεύτερος (deúteros, “second”) + νόμος (nómos, “law”) + -ιον (-ion). Translates Biblical Hebrew מִשְׁנֵה הַתּוֹרָה (mišnê hattôrâ).
